cards.title: Supercubic uniform formula lower bounds for SAT
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant ε>0 such that no LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family computing SATₙ for every n has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves?
cards.why: Would cross the cubic exponent for uniform De Morgan formula lower bounds on SAT. This quantifies a limitation of tree-shaped Boolean computation on an NP-complete problem without demanding a full separation from every polynomial-size family.

upgraded_from.title: Supercubic uniform formula lower bounds for SAT

cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for xᵢ, 1 for ¬xᵢ), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: ⌊log₂i⌋ zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. SATₙ:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with AND and OR gates of fan-in two. Each leaf is an input bit, its negation, or a Boolean constant. Equivalently, unary NOT gates can be used anywhere and then pushed to the leaves without changing the leaf count. Internal computations cannot be shared between two parents. Its size is the number of leaf occurrences, so repeated uses of the same variable are charged separately. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in O(log n) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and O(log n)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent ε is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves if some constant C bounds its size by Cn^(3+ε) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and ε, but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed ε>0 for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family has, for every C>0 and every N₀, some n≥N₀ with more than Cn^(3+ε) leaves. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every ε>0 some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has O(n^(3+ε)) leaves. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.

context_blocks.title: A quantitative lower bound for satisfiability
context_blocks.text: The object computing SAT receives the bits of a formula and outputs whether some assignment satisfies it. This card asks whether even a uniformly described De Morgan formula must exceed the n^3 scale by a fixed positive exponent. The circuit or formula that decides SAT is distinct from the 3-CNF formula encoded in its input.

context_blocks.title: What is being counted
context_blocks.text: The formula (a∧b)∨(a∧c) has four leaf occurrences, although it mentions only three variables. This illustrates why a formula-size bound counts uses of inputs, not distinct variable names. The benchmark size is for the formula computing SAT on n encoding bits.

context_blocks.title: Uniformity constrains the whole family
context_blocks.text: A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. The input to that description algorithm is the input length and a position in the description, not a particular SAT instance.

context_blocks.title: A fixed exponent, with a stated asymptotic convention
context_blocks.text: The question is whether SAT lies outside the uniform size-O(n^(3+ε)) class for some fixed ε>0. Thus every correct uniform family must exceed any constant multiple of that bound at arbitrarily large lengths. This uses the standard class-nonmembership interpretation of the source’s lower-bound question; it does not add an almost-everywhere requirement.

context_blocks.title: Dated progress and its scope
context_blocks.text: The 2016 column records nearly cubic De Morgan formula lower bounds for SAT. Bathie and Williams’s ITCS 2024 paper obtains a depth lower bound of 3.603 log₂ n for polylogtime-uniform NAND circuits solving SAT. NAND depth uses a restricted gate basis and a different cost measure; this statement alone does not settle the requested De Morgan leaf-size bound.

cards.title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
cards.formal: For every space-constructible function s:ℕ→ℕ with s(n)≥⌈log₂(n+2)⌉, is every language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) decidable deterministically in o(s(n)²) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an O(s(n))-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace g_D(n) on n-bit inputs satisfies lim(n→∞) g_D(n)/s(n)²=0?
cards.why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.
cards.status_note: Full source question read and standard space conventions made explicit. Subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no unconditional resolution of the displayed general containment. Related 2025 conditional results and 2026 catalytic-memory results were checked at abstract level; full proofs were not audited.

progress.text: Savitch proves the quadratic-space simulation; the original theorem is cited and restated in the 2025 source. The 1970 article was not independently retrieved for this review.

Mertz asks for the general containment NSPACE[s]⊆SPACE[o(s²)].
The separate connectivity work reports conditional and disjunctive consequences involving Savitch-type improvements.

upgraded_from.title: Improving SPACE versus NSPACE via Tree Evaluation

cards.definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. NSPACE(O(s(n))) denotes languages with such a machine using at most C s(n) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on 1ⁿ can output 1^s(n) using O(s(n)) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving s^(2−ε) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of s(n)². Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in NSPACE(O(s(n))) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in s(n)², a simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.title: What nondeterminism costs in memory
context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic machine can choose among several next moves and accepts if some sequence of choices succeeds. A deterministic simulation must decide the same question without those choices. Savitch’s theorem shows that squaring the workspace is enough, even though the simulation may take much longer.

context_blocks.title: Any vanishing fraction would count
context_blocks.text: If a nondeterministic computation uses about s cells, the target is a deterministic simulation whose memory divided by s² tends to zero. A bound such as s²/log(s+2) would qualify, while 0.01s² would not. These expressions illustrate the meaning of little-o; the question imposes no particular rate of improvement.

context_blocks.title: The logarithmic-space case
context_blocks.text: For s(n) of order log n, the target becomes deterministic o(log² n) space for every language in nondeterministic logarithmic space. This includes directed reachability: given a directed graph and two vertices, decide whether there is a directed path between them. The full card quantifies over all admitted s and does not restrict inputs to a special graph family.

context_blocks.title: Where tree evaluation fits in the history
context_blocks.text: The source was posed after Cook and Mertz’s STOC 2024 improvement for tree evaluation. That problem evaluates a tree of explicitly supplied functions and leaf values, and its stated space bound is O(log N·log log N) in the tree-evaluation input size N. The general nondeterministic-space simulation remains the target of the 2025 question.

context_blocks.title: Conditional progress
context_blocks.text: The 2025 connectivity paper states alternatives linking improvements in reachability and derandomization. Its abstract does not give an unconditional simulation of every nondeterministic-space computation in o(s²) space.

context_blocks.title: Catalytic memory is an additional resource
context_blocks.text: A 2026 directed-reachability preprint trades ordinary workspace against catalytic memory, which begins with arbitrary contents and must be restored. Its abstract does not state the requested improvement in total ordinary workspace.

cards.title: Stronger uniform depth-three majority lower bounds for SAT
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant ε>0 such that no LOGTIME-uniform depth-three MAJORITY/NOT circuit family computing SATₙ for every n has O(n^(5/2+ε)) wires?

cards.title: Explicit polynomial-separation lower bounds
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Source target, pending the coefficient convention described below: does there exist an explicit Boolean-function family f=(fₙ), in the book’s NP sense, which has no family of low-degree, low-weight polynomials separating its 1-inputs from its 0-inputs? “Separating” means pₙ(x)≠pₙ(y) whenever fₙ(x)=1 and fₙ(y)=0. The intended small-parameter regime is degree at most d(n) and weight at most 2^d(n), for some d(n)=(log n)^O(1).
cards.why: Studies whether Boolean answers can be encoded by algebraically simple numerical values that keep yes and no inputs disjoint. The source ties the question to restricted circuit lower bounds, but that significance depends on a consistent choice of coefficients and weight; it is not a generic polynomial-approximation problem.
cards.status_note: The intended measure is now recovered, but the coefficient/weight convention requires clarification before a theorem can be certified as matching the source target. Later searches through 11 September 2026 found no directly applicable correction or resolution. The credential-protected second-edition draft was not accessed, and the surrounding circuit lemma was not accepted as proved by this review.

sentences: The source asks for an NP Boolean-function family whose yes inputs and no inputs cannot be separated by low-degree, low-weight polynomial values.
Separation means that no yes input and no input receive the same value, rather than that a sign threshold computes the function.
The book supplies a precise certificate-based meaning of explicitness.
Its early draft conflicts over whether coefficients must remain in {−1,0,+1} or may include accumulated multiplicities.
The card now explains the question and its circuit motivation while retaining that coefficient convention as an unresolved formulation issue.

cards.definitions: For n≥2, fₙ maps {0,1}ⁿ to {0,1}. The book defines explicitness by a uniform polynomial-time Boolean verifier V and a polynomial q: fₙ(x)=1 exactly when V(x,y)=1 for some binary certificate y of length at most q(n). Thus the family’s accepted strings form a language in NP; merely giving an unbounded-time enumeration does not meet the source convention. A multilinear real polynomial has form p(x)=∑(S⊆{1,…,n}) a_S∏(i∈S)xᵢ, with the empty product equal to 1. It separates fₙ if the two sets {p(x):fₙ(x)=0} and {p(x):fₙ(x)=1} are disjoint; it need not approximate fₙ or classify inputs by the sign of p. In the draft’s literal definition each a_S belongs to {−1,0,+1}, degree is the largest |S| with a_S≠0, and weight is the number of nonzero a_S (degree and weight of the zero polynomial are taken as zero). Small degree/weight means that there exist fixed c≥1 and C≥1 such that, for all sufficiently large n, one can choose pₙ with degree at most d(n)=C(log₂ n)^c and weight at most 2^d(n). The separators need not be generated uniformly. If the literal coefficient convention is retained, a hard family would have, for every c,C and arbitrarily large n, no separator meeting both bounds. The alternative convention suggested by the draft’s addition step allows integer coefficients and counts ∑S |a_S| instead. The source does not clearly reconcile these conventions, so the accepted polynomial class remains a formulation gap.
cards.answer_criterion: Once the source’s polynomial coefficient and weight convention is settled, exhibit an NP family with no separating family in the specified low-degree/low-weight regime and prove the claimed lower bound, or prove that every NP family has such separators. The supplied source currently does not support choosing one of the two conflicting polynomial classes as the final benchmark theorem.

context_blocks.title: A number that distinguishes the two answers
context_blocks.text: A separating polynomial may assign many different numbers to yes inputs and many different numbers to no inputs. It only has to avoid assigning the same number to inputs with different answers. For example, x₁+x₂ separates two-bit parity: the even-parity inputs have values 0 or 2, and the odd-parity inputs have value 1. No single numerical threshold separates those two sets.

context_blocks.title: Why both degree and weight matter
context_blocks.text: Degree limits how many input coordinates can participate in a monomial. Weight limits the polynomial’s algebraic description according to the chosen coefficient convention. Without coefficient restrictions, x₁+2x₂+4x₃+⋯+2^(n−1)xₙ takes a different value on every Boolean input and therefore separates every Boolean function. The weight convention is consequently central to the question.

context_blocks.title: Explicit has a computational meaning here
context_blocks.text: The book’s definition asks for membership in NP, expressed by one polynomial-time certificate verifier. It does not require the function itself to be computable deterministically in polynomial time. This distinction is stated in Section 1.5.1 and is part of the recovered problem.

context_blocks.title: The source’s circuit motivation
context_blocks.text: The draft places this question after a claimed easy-separation property of ACC⁰: polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean circuits with AND, OR, NOT and modular-counting gates for fixed moduli. The coefficient inconsistency in that lemma prevents this review from treating the claimed implication as verified for the literal ±1 model.

context_blocks.title: Why this formulation remains unfinished
context_blocks.text: Adding x₁ to x₁ yields 2x₁, whose coefficient is outside {−1,0,+1}. The draft’s motivating proof sums polynomials but still calls the result a ±1 polynomial. Keeping distinct signed summands would instead produce an integer-coefficient polynomial with multiplicities. This card records the conflict so that the lower-bound target can be fixed without silently changing the source.

notes: Recovered the primary polynomial-separation measure and the book’s NP definition of explicitness.
Detected an unresolved discrepancy between the coefficient definition and the motivating addition argument.
statement_review.remaining_issue: The primary draft defines separating polynomials with combined coefficients in {−1,0,+1} and weight equal to the number of nonzero monomials. Its motivating ACC⁰ lemma then adds many such polynomials and calls the sum a ±1 polynomial, although repeated monomials can produce coefficients of magnitude greater than one. It is unclear whether the intended question retains the literal coefficient restriction or allows integer coefficients with weight charged by multiplicity/total absolute coefficient. These are different lower-bound targets. The public errata did not settle the convention; the card does not silently select a correction.

changes: Recovered the previously missing algebraic separation measure and computational explicitness requirement.
Added concrete examples distinguishing separation from threshold representation.
Recorded the source coefficient inconsistency instead of inventing a corrected lower-bound target.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
